menu.tip:
Line  L

Draws a straight bar between two points. It is a real 2D solid (a hull of two circles), so it can be extruded like any shape.

How to use

  1. Press where the line starts.
  2. Drag to the end point — the length shows in the status bar.
  3. Release. Set its thickness (Width) in Properties.
  4. Use Extrude to turn it into a 3D rod or wall.

Tip: Turn Snap on to land the ends on round grid values.
menu.status: Line — Draws a straight bar between two points. It is a real 2D solid (a hull of two circles), so it can be extruded like any shape.

menu.tip:
Rectangle  R

Draws a rectangle on the sketch plane — the usual start of a plate, a box or a bracket.

How to use

  1. Press at one corner.
  2. Drag to the opposite corner; the size reads live in mm.
  3. Release, then type exact Width/Height in Properties.
  4. Extrude it to give it thickness.
menu.status: Rectangle — Draws a rectangle on the sketch plane — the usual start of a plate, a box or a bracket.

menu.tip:
Circle  C

Draws a circle, or a part of one (a quarter, a semicircle) — rods, discs, holes and arcs.

How to use

  1. Press at the centre.
  2. Drag outwards to the radius (r and Ø show live).
  3. Release. In Properties, Angle 180 makes a semicircle, 90 a quarter; Segments sets how smooth it is.

Tip: A circle inside a Difference cuts a round hole.
menu.status: Circle — Draws a circle, or a part of one (a quarter, a semicircle) — rods, discs, holes and arcs.

menu.tip:
Polygon  P

Draws any straight-sided outline, one corner at a time — gussets, profiles, custom brackets.

How to use

  1. Click each corner in turn.
  2. Double-click (or press Enter) to close the shape — at least three corners.
  3. Esc abandons it.
  4. Edit any corner exactly in the points table in Properties.
menu.status: Polygon — Draws any straight-sided outline, one corner at a time — gussets, profiles, custom brackets.

menu.tip:
Text  T

Places a line of lettering on the sketch — labels, name plates, stamps.

How to use

  1. Click where the text should start.
  2. Type the words and the Size in Properties.
  3. Extrude it to make raised or engraved lettering.

Tip: Put extruded text in a Difference to engrave it into a part.
menu.status: Text — Places a line of lettering on the sketch — labels, name plates, stamps.

menu.tip:
Cube (box)

Adds a box — the most common starting block.

How to use

  1. Click. In the Main tab it becomes a new Object and the Object tab opens on it; in the Object tab it is added to the part you are editing.
  2. Set Width (X), Depth (Y) and Height (Z) in Properties.
  3. X/Y/Z move it; Center puts its middle on that point instead of its corner.
menu.status: Cube (box) — Adds a box — the most common starting block.

menu.tip:
Sphere

Adds a ball — eyes, knobs, joints, domes.

How to use

  1. Click to add it at the origin (see Cube for where it lands).
  2. Set the Radius; X/Y/Z move its centre.
  3. Segments sets smoothness (more = rounder, slower).
menu.status: Sphere — Adds a ball — eyes, knobs, joints, domes.

menu.tip:
Cylinder / cone

Adds a cylinder — shafts, legs, pins, holes. A different top radius makes a cone (0 comes to a point).

How to use

  1. Click to add it (see Cube for where it lands).
  2. Set Height and the bottom and top radius.
  3. Center stands it on its middle instead of its base.

Tip: Inside a Difference, a cylinder drills a hole.
menu.status: Cylinder / cone — Adds a cylinder — shafts, legs, pins, holes. A different top radius makes a cone (0 comes to a point).

menu.tip:
Capsule

A rod with rounded ends between two points — arms, legs, fingers, handles.

How to use

  1. Click to add it.
  2. Set the Start and End points and the Radius.
  3. Wrap it in a Joint to pose it, or a Blend to melt it into a body.
menu.status: Capsule — A rod with rounded ends between two points — arms, legs, fingers, handles.

menu.tip:
Ellipsoid

A sphere stretched differently along X, Y and Z — heads, bodies, eggs, pebbles.

How to use

  1. Click to add it.
  2. Set Radius X, Y and Z; Centre X/Y/Z moves it.
menu.status: Ellipsoid — A sphere stretched differently along X, Y and Z — heads, bodies, eggs, pebbles.

menu.tip:
Rounded box

A box whose edges and corners are rounded — cases, buttons, soft blocks.

How to use

  1. Click to add it.
  2. Set Width, Depth, Height and the Edge radius (0 = sharp).
menu.status: Rounded box — A box whose edges and corners are rounded — cases, buttons, soft blocks.

menu.tip:
Loft (tube through sections)

A smooth tube that passes through a list of cross-sections — tails, necks, horns, bent handles, ducts.

How to use

  1. Click to add it.
  2. In Properties, each Sections row is one ring: its centre X, Y, Z and its two radii. Add rows to lengthen it.
  3. Smoothing rounds the path; Ends picks round or flat caps.
menu.status: Loft (tube through sections) — A smooth tube that passes through a list of cross-sections — tails, necks, horns, bent handles, ducts.

menu.tip:
Skin (body round a skeleton)

Draw a stick skeleton — points with a thickness, each joined to its parent — and get one smooth body round it, limbs tapering and joints blending like flesh. Like Blender's Skin modifier.

How to use

  1. Click Skin: a two-point stub appears.
  2. In Properties, add skeleton rows: a point (x, y, z), the body's radius there, and the row it joins to (-1 for the root) — a spine, a neck and head, two arms, two legs, a tail.
  3. Pose rows turn everything beyond a point (rx, ry, rz): the body is grown again round the posed skeleton, so it stays whole.
  4. Blend joints over sets how soft armpits and hips are; Detail how fine the surface is.

Tip: Then Sculpt it for muscle, Displace for scales — or Armature ▸ from the skin's skeleton to pose it after sculpting.
menu.status: Skin (body round a skeleton) — Draw a stick skeleton — points with a thickness, each joined to its parent — and get one smooth body round it, limbs tapering and joints blending like flesh. Like Blender's Skin modifier.

items.tip:
SubD (smooth cage)

A smooth surface shaped by a coarse cage — Rhino's SubD. Eight cage points make a pebble; a few dozen make a shoe, a car body, a head.

How to use

  1. Insert ▸ SubD Box, or select a solid and Tools ▸ Convert to SubD.
  2. Press Tab over the 3D view: Edit Mode opens the CAGE. Drag points, E extrudes a face, the surface follows.
  3. Smoothness, crease angle and creased edges are in Properties.

Tip: Tick Show the cage too to see it while you work outside Edit Mode.
items.status: SubD (smooth cage) — A smooth surface shaped by a coarse cage — Rhino's SubD. Eight cage points make a pebble; a few dozen make a shoe, a car body, a head.

items.tip:
Draw 3D curve  Ctrl+Alt+C

Click points in the 3D view to draw a smooth curve through them. Points SNAP to corners, the middle of edges, edges and surfaces — the marker says which — or land on the ground grid in empty space.

How to use

  1. Insert ▸ Draw 3D Curve, or Ctrl+Alt+C.
  2. Click each point. Hold Shift to go straight up or down from the last point; hold Alt to switch snapping off.
  3. Or just type a point — 10, 20, 5 — or @0, 0, 15 for 15 above the last one, then Enter.
  4. Enter, right-click or double-click finishes; Backspace takes a point back; C (or clicking the first point) closes a loop.

Tip: Dragging still turns the view, so you can look round between clicks.
items.status: Draw 3D curve — Click points in the 3D view to draw a smooth curve through them. Points SNAP to corners, the middle of edges, edges and surfaces — the marker says which — or land on the ground grid in empty space.

menu.tip:
For loop (repeat)

Repeats its contents: the variable runs From → To by Step, or through a list of Values (like 0, 90, 180).

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) to repeat and click For loop — or click with nothing selected and drag objects into the empty loop.
  2. Set the Variable name (i) and its range.
  3. Use it in any field: X = i * 20, Rotate Z = i * 45.

Tip: Loops nest: a loop in a loop makes a grid.
menu.status: For loop (repeat) — Repeats its contents: the variable runs From → To by Step, or through a list of Values (like 0, 90, 180).

menu.tip:
While loop

Repeats while a condition holds: the variable starts at the Initial value and is updated each time round.

How to use

  1. Select what to repeat (or nothing, for an empty loop) and click While loop.
  2. Set e.g. Variable x, Initial 1, Condition x < 100, Update x * 2.
  3. Use the variable in the contents' fields.

Tip: Capped at 1000 rounds; written out as a list for OpenSCAD.
menu.status: While loop — Repeats while a condition holds: the variable starts at the Initial value and is updated each time round.

menu.tip:
If / else

Shows its contents only when the condition is true, and the Else branch otherwise — options and alternating patterns.

How to use

  1. Select the objects (or nothing) and click If / else.
  2. Type a Condition: with_lid, or i % 2 == 0 inside a loop.
  3. Put the alternative inside the Else row.
menu.status: If / else — Shows its contents only when the condition is true, and the Else branch otherwise — options and alternating patterns.

menu.tip:
Pattern (linear / polar / grid)

Repeats its contents as copies — in a row, round an axis, or on a grid — like Blender's Array or a SolidWorks pattern. A bolt circle, a row of holes, a spiral stair, a peg board.

How to use

  1. Select what to repeat and click Pattern (or click with nothing selected and drag objects into the empty pattern).
  2. Choose the Kind: linear (Count copies at Step X/Y/Z), polar (Count copies turned about the Axis over Angle°) or grid (Count X/Y/Z at Step X/Y/Z).
  3. Polar: Angle 360 spreads the copies evenly round the circle; below 360 they span the angle, first at 0°, last at Angle. Rise per copy lifts each one along the axis — a helix.

Tip: Every field takes an expression, so a pattern inside a loop can read the loop variable. Capped at 1000 copies.
menu.status: Pattern (linear / polar / grid) — Repeats its contents as copies — in a row, round an axis, or on a grid — like Blender's Array or a SolidWorks pattern. A bolt circle, a row of holes, a spiral stair, a peg board.

menu.tip:
Scatter on surface

Copies one piece over a surface — spikes down a spine, warts, scales, barnacles, rows of teeth, eye clusters, rivets. Like Blender's particles: each copy stands along the surface normal, sized and turned a little at random.

How to use

  1. Model the piece at the origin standing up along +Z, base at z = 0 (a cone for a spike).
  2. Select the piece, then the body (Ctrl+click), and click Scatter: the first child is the piece, the rest the surface.
  3. In Properties: how many copies and how far apart, size and its variation, random spin and lean, sink into the surface, only faces looking one way, or a region.
  4. Mode Path puts the copies evenly along points you give — a spine, a jaw line — each dropped onto the surface; Taper makes them smaller towards the ends.

Tip: Edit the piece and every copy follows. Sink a little so no gap shows under a copy on a curved body.
menu.status: Scatter on surface — Copies one piece over a surface — spikes down a spine, warts, scales, barnacles, rows of teeth, eye clusters, rivets. Like Blender's particles: each copy stands along the surface normal, sized and turned a little at random.

menu.tip:
Intersection for

A for loop whose copies are INTERSECTED instead of joined: only the volume every iteration shares remains. Three boxes turned 60° apart intersect into a hexagonal prism.

How to use

  1. Select what to repeat and click Intersection for (or click with nothing selected and drag objects in).
  2. Set the Variable and its range (From, To, Step) or a list of Values.
  3. Use the variable in the contents, e.g. a Rotate Z of i.

Tip: The built-in preview draws the first iteration; the OpenSCAD render shows the true intersection.
menu.status: Intersection for — A for loop whose copies are INTERSECTED instead of joined: only the volume every iteration shares remains. Three boxes turned 60° apart intersect into a hexagonal prism.

menu.tip:
Let (local variables)

Names values for what it holds only — OpenSCAD's let(). Work a radius out once from a diameter and use it in every child.

How to use

  1. Select the objects and click Let (or insert an empty one and drag objects in).
  2. Write the bindings: r = d / 2, h = r * 3 — later ones may use earlier ones.
  3. Type the names into the children's fields (Radius: r).

Tip: The names exist only inside the Let; a Variable at the top level is seen everywhere.
menu.status: Let (local variables) — Names values for what it holds only — OpenSCAD's let(). Work a radius out once from a diameter and use it in every child.

menu.tip:
Variable

Adds or applies Variable.
menu.status: Variable — Adds or applies Variable.

menu.tip:
Echo (print)

OpenSCAD's echo(): prints values to OpenSCAD's console when the program runs — to check a computed size or a loop count.

How to use

  1. Insert ▸ Code & files ▸ Echo.
  2. Write the arguments as in OpenSCAD: "width = ", w, area = w * h.

Tip: A named argument prints as name = value.
menu.status: Echo (print) — OpenSCAD's echo(): prints values to OpenSCAD's console when the program runs — to check a computed size or a loop count.

menu.tip:
Assert (check)

OpenSCAD's assert(): stops the program with a message when a condition is false. In KherveCAD the node turns red at once, with the message, so a parameter out of range is caught while editing.

How to use

  1. Insert ▸ Code & files ▸ Assert.
  2. Write the Condition (wall >= 1.2) and a Message — an expression, so str("wall ", wall, " is too thin") works.

Tip: Put asserts next to the Variables they guard.
menu.status: Assert (check) — OpenSCAD's assert(): stops the program with a message when a condition is false. In KherveCAD the node turns red at once, with the message, so a parameter out of range is caught while editing.

menu.tip:
Import STL

Adds or applies Import STL.
menu.status: Import STL — Adds or applies Import STL.

menu.tip:
OpenSCAD code

Adds or applies OpenSCAD code.
menu.status: OpenSCAD code — Adds or applies OpenSCAD code.

menu.tip:
Sheet metal part

Adds or applies Sheet metal part.
menu.status: Sheet metal part — Adds or applies Sheet metal part.

menu.tip:
Gear (involute)

A true involute gear by module, tooth count and pressure angle — spur, helical, herringbone, internal (ring), rack, bevel or worm — with bore, backlash and root clearance. Two gears of the same module and pressure angle mesh at a centre distance of m (z1 + z2) / 2.

How to use

  1. Insert ▸ Mechanical features ▸ Gear.
  2. Choose the Kind, then the Module (tooth size) and Teeth.
  3. Set Thickness, a Bore, and for a helical or herringbone gear the Helix angle; a bevel gear needs its mate's tooth count.
  4. Print-in-place pairs want 0.1–0.2 mm of Backlash.

Tip: Every field takes an expression, so teeth = ratio * 10 keeps a pair in step; the code is kcad_gear(...), real OpenSCAD.
menu.status: Gear (involute) — A true involute gear by module, tooth count and pressure angle — spur, helical, herringbone, internal (ring), rack, bevel or worm — with bore, backlash and root clearance. Two gears of the same module and pressure angle mesh at a centre distance of m (z1 + z2) / 2.

menu.tip:
Thread (screw thread)

A real helical screw thread — ISO metric, trapezoidal, square, buttress, tapered pipe or bottle neck — male, or as the slightly larger tap you subtract to make a nut or a threaded hole. Any number of starts, right or left hand.

How to use

  1. Insert ▸ Mechanical features ▸ Thread.
  2. Set the Profile, Major diameter, Pitch and Length (M8: 8 mm, 1.25).
  3. For a nut or a threaded hole tick Internal and put the thread inside a Difference with the part; 0.2 mm Clearance prints well.

Tip: A thread is a twisted cross-section, so it previews exactly and renders fast — no boolean inside.
menu.status: Thread (screw thread) — A real helical screw thread — ISO metric, trapezoidal, square, buttress, tapered pipe or bottle neck — male, or as the slightly larger tap you subtract to make a nut or a threaded hole. Any number of starts, right or left hand.

menu.tip:
Hole (counterbore, countersink, nut trap…)

The solid to cut for a fastener: plain, counterbore, countersink, nut trap, heat-set insert, slot, or a teardrop that prints horizontally without support. Its top sits at z = 0 and it goes down, so it drops onto a face.

How to use

  1. Insert ▸ Mechanical features ▸ Hole.
  2. Pick the Kind and the sizes (M3: 3.2 mm hole, 6 mm head).
  3. Move it onto the face, then select it with the part and click Difference.

Tip: Extends above the face keeps the cut clean on a flush face; the teardrop runs along X with its point up.
menu.status: Hole (counterbore, countersink, nut trap…) — The solid to cut for a fastener: plain, counterbore, countersink, nut trap, heat-set insert, slot, or a teardrop that prints horizontally without support. Its top sits at z = 0 and it goes down, so it drops onto a face.

menu.tip:
Knurled cylinder

A cylinder covered in diamond knurling — two sets of helical grooves crossing — for a knob or a thumb screw you can grip.

How to use

  1. Insert ▸ Mechanical features ▸ Knurled cylinder.
  2. Set the Outer diameter and Length, how many Diamonds round and the Groove depth (0.6–1 mm prints well).

Tip: Put it in a Group with the knob's other shapes; the helix angle sets how tall the diamonds are.
menu.status: Knurled cylinder — A cylinder covered in diamond knurling — two sets of helical grooves crossing — for a knob or a thumb screw you can grip.

menu.tip:
Textured cylinder / panel

A cylinder or a flat panel with a relief pattern on its surface — ribs, waves, diamonds, bricks, hexagons, dimples or checkers — for grips, lids, lithophane-like panels and decoration.

How to use

  1. Insert ▸ Mechanical features ▸ Textured cylinder / panel.
  2. Choose the Shape and the Pattern, then its size (Pattern size) and how deep it goes (Relief depth).
  3. Raise Samples per pattern for a smoother relief.

Tip: Round a cylinder the pattern size is adjusted so it closes without a seam.
menu.status: Textured cylinder / panel — A cylinder or a flat panel with a relief pattern on its surface — ribs, waves, diamonds, bricks, hexagons, dimples or checkers — for grips, lids, lithophane-like panels and decoration.

menu.tip:
3D curve

A smooth (or straight) line through points in space, drawn as a round wire — a cable, a handrail, a bent rod, a coil, the rail for a sweep. Exported to STEP as an exact B-spline pipe.

How to use

  1. Insert ▸ Shapes & patterns ▸ 3D curve.
  2. Edit the Points table: one row per point it passes through (X, Y, Z). Add rows to add bends.
  3. Pick Smooth or Straight, tick Closed loop for a ring, and set the Wire thickness.
  4. Right-click ▸ Make a Sweep Along This Curve to give it any profile.

Tip: Thin it right down and hide it to keep it as a guide.
menu.status: 3D curve — A smooth (or straight) line through points in space, drawn as a round wire — a cable, a handrail, a bent rod, a coil, the rail for a sweep. Exported to STEP as an exact B-spline pipe.

menu.tip:
Regular polyhedron

A Platonic or Archimedean solid — tetrahedron to icosahedron, cuboctahedron, the football (truncated icosahedron) and more — sized by the sphere through its corners.

How to use

  1. Insert ▸ Shapes & patterns ▸ Regular polyhedron.
  2. Pick the Solid and its Circumradius.

Tip: Dice, lamp shades, a geodesic starting point.
menu.status: Regular polyhedron — A Platonic or Archimedean solid — tetrahedron to icosahedron, cuboctahedron, the football (truncated icosahedron) and more — sized by the sphere through its corners.

menu.tip:
Regular polygon / star

A 2D regular polygon, or a star of that many tips between an outer and an inner radius.

How to use

  1. Insert ▸ Shapes & patterns ▸ Regular polygon / star.
  2. Set Sides / tips and the Outer radius; an Inner radius of 0 gives the plain polygon.
  3. Extrude it for a solid.

Tip: Turn° sets where the first tip points (90 = up).
menu.status: Regular polygon / star — A 2D regular polygon, or a star of that many tips between an outer and an inner radius.

menu.tip:
Rounded polygon (radius per corner)

A 2D outline whose every corner has its own fillet radius — a bracket profile with a big inside radius and small outside ones, in one shape (Round-Anything's polyRound).

How to use

  1. Insert ▸ Shapes & patterns ▸ Rounded polygon.
  2. Edit the Corners table: X, Y and the Radius of each corner (0 keeps it sharp).
  3. Extrude it.

Tip: A radius too big for a short edge is shrunk to fit.
menu.status: Rounded polygon (radius per corner) — A 2D outline whose every corner has its own fillet radius — a bracket profile with a big inside radius and small outside ones, in one shape (Round-Anything's polyRound).

menu.tip:
Bézier shape (closed)

A smooth 2D outline of cubic Bézier curves — a logo, a cam, a guitar body.

How to use

  1. Insert ▸ Shapes & patterns ▸ Bézier shape.
  2. Rows come in threes: a point on the curve, then two control points pulling the curve toward the next point.
  3. Extrude it.

Tip: The last curve closes back to the first point.
menu.status: Bézier shape (closed) — A smooth 2D outline of cubic Bézier curves — a logo, a cam, a guitar body.

menu.tip:
SVG path shape

A 2D shape typed as an SVG path — M, L, H, V, C, S, Q, T, A and Z, absolute or relative — so curves and arcs are one line of text. A subpath inside another is a hole.

How to use

  1. Insert ▸ Shapes & patterns ▸ SVG path shape.
  2. Type the path: M 0 0 L 40 0 A 10 10 0 0 1 40 20 L 0 20 Z.
  3. Extrude it.

Tip: y runs up, as everywhere in KherveCAD (not down as in an SVG file).
menu.status: SVG path shape — A 2D shape typed as an SVG path — M, L, H, V, C, S, Q, T, A and Z, absolute or relative — so curves and arcs are one line of text. A subpath inside another is a hole.

menu.tip:
Honeycomb panel (2D)

A rectangle perforated with hexagonal cells — extrude it for a light, stiff, printable panel or grille.

How to use

  1. Insert ▸ Shapes & patterns ▸ Honeycomb panel.
  2. Set the Width, Height, Cell size, Wall between cells and the solid Margin.
  3. Extrude it.

Tip: Only whole cells are cut, so the edge stays solid.
menu.status: Honeycomb panel (2D) — A rectangle perforated with hexagonal cells — extrude it for a light, stiff, printable panel or grille.

menu.tip:
Linear extrude

Turns a flat 2D shape into a solid by pushing it straight up (along Z).

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. Pick 2D shapes: rectangle, circle, polygon, text or line.
  2. Click Linear extrude.
  3. Set Height. Optional: Twist (degrees over the height), Scale (top size vs bottom, 0 = a point), Center (extrude both ways).

Tip: Only 2D shapes can go inside — a 3D object there turns red.
menu.status: Linear extrude — Turns a flat 2D shape into a solid by pushing it straight up (along Z).

menu.tip:
Rotate extrude (lathe)

Spins a 2D profile round the Z axis like a lathe — cups, flanges, bottles, wheels.

How to use

  1. Draw HALF the cross-section, to the right of the vertical axis (X ≥ 0): X becomes the radius, Y the height.
  2. Select it and click Rotate extrude.
  3. Angle below 360 makes a partial revolve (a slice).

Tip: A profile crossing X = 0 turns red — keep it on one side.
menu.status: Rotate extrude (lathe) — Spins a 2D profile round the Z axis like a lathe — cups, flanges, bottles, wheels.

menu.tip:
Sweep along path

Drives a flat 2D profile along a 3D path — pipes, handrails, cable runs, springs, chain links. Corners are mitred and the path can be smoothed into a curve.

How to use

  1. Draw the cross-section as 2D shapes (a circle for a pipe, a rectangle for a rail) around the origin: seen with the path coming towards you, x is right and y is up.
  2. Select it and click Sweep along path.
  3. In Properties, type the Path points (X, Y, Z) the profile should follow; Smoothing rounds the corners into a curve.
  4. Wall thickness > 0 makes it hollow (a pipe); Closed loop joins the end to the start (an O-ring); Twist and Scale act over the length.

Tip: Only 2D shapes go inside. The result is baked into the program, so a sweep cannot sit inside a loop — put the loop inside the sweep instead.
menu.status: Sweep along path — Drives a flat 2D profile along a 3D path — pipes, handrails, cable runs, springs, chain links. Corners are mitred and the path can be smoothed into a curve.

menu.tip:
Loft through sections

Joins a series of 2D shapes — one cross-section each — into one solid, keeping their corners as sharp edges: car bodies, boat hulls, bottles with flats, wings.

How to use

  1. Draw each cross-section as a polygon (or rectangle, circle) in the XY plane, around the same origin.
  2. Select them in order and click Loft through sections.
  3. In Properties, type one height (Z) per section, in the same order as the shapes in the tree.
  4. Smoothing adds curved in-between sections; the ones you drew stay exactly where they are.

Tip: Give every section the same number of points and they join point to point, so each corner runs as a crisp edge. Rotate the loft to make it run along X.
menu.status: Loft through sections — Joins a series of 2D shapes — one cross-section each — into one solid, keeping their corners as sharp edges: car bodies, boat hulls, bottles with flats, wings.

menu.tip:
Translate (move)

Moves the selection by X, Y and Z millimetres.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view.
  2. Click Translate.
  3. Type the X/Y/Z offsets.

Tip: Primitives already have their own X/Y/Z, and dragging in the 2D view moves too — Translate is for moving a whole group.
menu.status: Translate (move) — Moves the selection by X, Y and Z millimetres.

menu.tip:
Rotate

Turns the selection about X, then Y, then Z (degrees), around the origin (0, 0, 0).

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view.
  2. Click Rotate.
  3. Type the angles.

Tip: It turns around the origin, so a part already moved away swings round: rotate first, then move.
menu.status: Rotate — Turns the selection about X, then Y, then Z (degrees), around the origin (0, 0, 0).

menu.tip:
Scale

Multiplies the selection's size along X, Y and Z (1 = unchanged, 2 = double, 0.5 = half).

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view.
  2. Click Scale.
  3. Type the factors.
menu.status: Scale — Multiplies the selection's size along X, Y and Z (1 = unchanged, 2 = double, 0.5 = half).

menu.tip:
Mirror

Reflects the selection across a plane. (1, 0, 0) swaps left and right, (0, 1, 0) front and back, (0, 0, 1) up and down.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view.
  2. Click Mirror.
  3. Set the plane's normal X/Y/Z.

Tip: The original is not kept — use Symmetry to keep both halves.
menu.status: Mirror — Reflects the selection across a plane. (1, 0, 0) swaps left and right, (0, 1, 0) front and back, (0, 0, 1) up and down.

menu.tip:
Resize (absolute size)

Scales what it holds to a size in millimetres rather than by a factor — OpenSCAD's resize(). Make a part exactly 40 mm long without working out the scale.

How to use

  1. Select the objects and click Resize.
  2. Type the new size along X, Y and/or Z; 0 keeps that axis.
  3. Tick Auto on an axis left at 0 to scale it with the others, keeping the proportions.

Tip: OpenSCAD scales about the origin, like scale(): centre the part first if it should grow evenly.
menu.status: Resize (absolute size) — Scales what it holds to a size in millimetres rather than by a factor — OpenSCAD's resize(). Make a part exactly 40 mm long without working out the scale.

menu.tip:
Matrix transform (multmatrix)

Applies a 4 x 4 affine matrix — the general transform that translate, rotate, scale, mirror and shear are all cases of. Every .csg file OpenSCAD writes places its shapes this way.

How to use

  1. Select the objects and click Matrix transform.
  2. Edit the rows: the first three columns turn, scale and shear; the fourth column moves (X, Y, Z).
  3. Leave the last row 0, 0, 0, 1.

Tip: Put a number off the diagonal (row 1, column 2) for a shear — something no other transform can do.
menu.status: Matrix transform (multmatrix) — Applies a 4 x 4 affine matrix — the general transform that translate, rotate, scale, mirror and shear are all cases of. Every .csg file OpenSCAD writes places its shapes this way.

menu.tip:
Group (union)  Ctrl+G

Joins the selection into one object, so it moves, colours and combines as one.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view.
  2. Click Group (Ctrl+G).
  3. Nothing selected? An empty group is added — drag objects into it in the tree.

Tip: Ctrl+Shift+G ungroups.
menu.status: Group (union) — Joins the selection into one object, so it moves, colours and combines as one.

menu.tip:
Difference (cut)

Cuts: keeps the FIRST object and subtracts everything after it — holes, slots, pockets, engraving.

How to use

  1. Select the body FIRST, then the cutting shapes.
  2. Click Difference.
  3. In the tree the first child is the body; drag to reorder if the wrong one is being cut.

Tip: Holes show cut only with the OpenSCAD engine (F5); the quick preview shows the body whole.
menu.status: Difference (cut) — Cuts: keeps the FIRST object and subtracts everything after it — holes, slots, pockets, engraving.

menu.tip:
Intersection

Keeps only the volume where ALL the selected objects overlap — rounded-off corners, lens shapes, trimming.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view.
  2. Click Intersection.
menu.status: Intersection — Keeps only the volume where ALL the selected objects overlap — rounded-off corners, lens shapes, trimming.

menu.tip:
Render (cache as mesh)

OpenSCAD's render(): tells OpenSCAD to compute its contents as one finished mesh in its own preview. The shape is unchanged; a complex boolean inside a loop previews faster.

How to use

  1. Select the objects and click Render.
  2. Raise Convexity if OpenSCAD's preview shows see-through faces (the most walls a ray can cross, halved).

Tip: KherveCAD's own preview ignores it; it is kept so the program reads the same in OpenSCAD.
menu.status: Render (cache as mesh) — OpenSCAD's render(): tells OpenSCAD to compute its contents as one finished mesh in its own preview. The shape is unchanged; a complex boolean inside a loop previews faster.

menu.tip:
Fillet edges (round / chamfer)

Rounds the edges you click — SolidWorks' Fillet. A convex edge is rounded off, an inside corner is filled in; Chamfer cuts a flat instead of a curve.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. Pick the solid (or several).
  2. Click Fillet edges: the 3D view asks for edges.
  3. Click an edge to round it; one click on a cylinder's rim takes the whole rim, a click on a face rounds every edge round that face. Esc or right-click when done.
  4. Set the Radius (or the chamfer's setback) in Properties. Right-click the fillet ▸ Pick edges to add more.

Tip: The rounding shows in the exact OpenSCAD render (a moment after each change, or F5) — the quick preview cannot cut.
menu.status: Fillet edges (round / chamfer) — Rounds the edges you click — SolidWorks' Fillet. A convex edge is rounded off, an inside corner is filled in; Chamfer cuts a flat instead of a curve.

menu.tip:
Bevel edges

Rounds or chamfers EVERY sharp edge of a part at once — outside edges, inside corners or both — with true rounded corners where three edges meet. The part keeps its size.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. Pick the part.
  2. Click Bevel edges.
  3. Width: the radius of the round (mm).
  4. Segments: steps across it (1 = a flat chamfer).
  5. Profile: 0.5 round, 0.25 flat, towards 1 squarer, lower a cove.
  6. Edges sharper than: leave gentle creases (a cylinder's facets) alone.

Tip: To round only some edges, use Fillet edges and click them.
menu.status: Bevel edges — Rounds or chamfers EVERY sharp edge of a part at once — outside edges, inside corners or both — with true rounded corners where three edges meet. The part keeps its size.

menu.tip:
Push / pull faces

Moves a flat face straight out (a boss, a taller wall) or in (a pocket, a recess), like SketchUp — with an optional inset that leaves a rim around it.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. Pick the part.
  2. Click Push / pull, then click flat faces in the 3D view.
  3. Each face comes out 5 mm: set its Distance in Properties (negative cuts in) and its Inset (a rim).
  4. Esc when done; right-click ▸ Pick faces to add more.

Tip: Faces apply in order: click the top you just raised to raise it again.
menu.status: Push / pull faces — Moves a flat face straight out (a boss, a taller wall) or in (a pocket, a recess), like SketchUp — with an optional inset that leaves a rim around it.

menu.tip:
Bisect (knife)

Cuts a part with a flat plane: keep the top, the bottom, or both halves pulled apart — to see inside, flatten a base, or split a part for printing.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. Pick the part.
  2. Click Bisect.
  3. Set the plane's point and normal (0, 0, 1 is a horizontal cut), and what to keep.
menu.status: Bisect (knife) — Cuts a part with a flat plane: keep the top, the bottom, or both halves pulled apart — to see inside, flatten a base, or split a part for printing.

menu.tip:
Hull (shrink-wrap)

Wraps the selection in the tightest convex skin — two spheres become a capsule, four pillars a rounded plate.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view.
  2. Click Hull.
  3. Move or resize the pieces inside; the skin follows.
menu.status: Hull (shrink-wrap) — Wraps the selection in the tightest convex skin — two spheres become a capsule, four pillars a rounded plate.

menu.tip:
Minkowski (sweep one shape round another)

Grows the first child by the shape of the second — a box plus a small sphere is a box with every edge rounded.

How to use

  1. Select the body FIRST, then the shape to sweep round it (a small sphere for rounding).
  2. Click Minkowski.

Tip: To round only chosen edges use Fillet edges instead; this rounds all of them and is slow on big parts.
menu.status: Minkowski (sweep one shape round another) — Grows the first child by the shape of the second — a box plus a small sphere is a box with every edge rounded.

menu.tip:
Smooth blend

Melts shapes together like clay: where they meet, the seam becomes a smooth fillet instead of a sharp crease.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. Use spheres, capsules, ellipsoids, boxes, rounded boxes or cylinders.
  2. Click Smooth blend.
  3. Blend radius sets how far the melting reaches; Detail sets the mesh resolution (higher = finer, slower).

Tip: A blend cannot sit inside a loop — the loop varies, the melted mesh cannot.
menu.status: Smooth blend — Melts shapes together like clay: where they meet, the seam becomes a smooth fillet instead of a sharp crease.

menu.tip:
Bend

Curves the selection along an arc — bananas, arches, curled tails.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view.
  2. Click Bend.
  3. Length axis = the long direction; Bend toward = which way it curls; Angle = the total bend.
  4. Max edge: smaller gives a smoother curve.
menu.status: Bend — Curves the selection along an arc — bananas, arches, curled tails.

menu.tip:
Twist

Wrings the selection around an axis, turning by Angle over its length — drills, twisted columns, horns.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view.
  2. Click Twist.
  3. Pick the Axis and the Angle.
menu.status: Twist — Wrings the selection around an axis, turning by Angle over its length — drills, twisted columns, horns.

menu.tip:
Taper

Shrinks (or grows) the selection towards its far end — pointed legs, tapered posts, fingers.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view.
  2. Click Taper.
  3. Pick the Axis; Scale at the far end: 0.5 = half size, 2 = double.
menu.status: Taper — Shrinks (or grows) the selection towards its far end — pointed legs, tapered posts, fingers.

menu.tip:
Lattice (free-form)

Free-form reshaping: move the 8 corners of the bounding box and the shape follows smoothly — squash, lean or bulge it.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view.
  2. Click Lattice.
  3. In Properties, each row moves one corner by dX, dY, dZ (row order: X changes fastest, then Y, then Z).
menu.status: Lattice (free-form) — Free-form reshaping: move the 8 corners of the bounding box and the shape follows smoothly — squash, lean or bulge it.

menu.tip:
Subdivide (smooth)

Smooths a blocky shape by splitting and relaxing every triangle — boxes turn into pebbles.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view.
  2. Click Subdivide.
  3. Levels 1–4: each level makes it smoother (and 4× heavier).
  4. Keep edges sharper than: 30–60° keeps a part's real edges crisp (a cylinder's rims, a box's corners) while its curved sides round off — 0 rounds everything.
menu.status: Subdivide (smooth) — Smooths a blocky shape by splitting and relaxing every triangle — boxes turn into pebbles.

menu.tip:
Decimate (fewer triangles)

Makes a heavy part light: fewer triangles, the same shape — a scan, a sculpt, a threaded part or a tree that slows the view or the export. Flat areas lose triangles first, detail last.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. Pick the heavy solid.
  2. Click Decimate.
  3. Keep: the fraction of triangles to keep (0.25 = a quarter).
  4. Or within: a distance in mm the surface may move instead — 0.05 is invisible on a print.

Tip: A closed solid stays closed, so it still prints.
menu.status: Decimate (fewer triangles) — Makes a heavy part light: fewer triangles, the same shape — a scan, a sculpt, a threaded part or a tree that slows the view or the export. Flat areas lose triangles first, detail last.

menu.tip:
Remesh (clean solid)

Rebuilds a messy part as ONE clean closed solid of even triangles: overlapping pieces merge, inner walls and small holes in a scan disappear. Use it when a part will not print, bevel, shrinkwrap or cut.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. Pick the messy part.
  2. Click Remesh.
  3. Voxel size: the detail kept (mm) — smaller is finer and heavier.
  4. Snap keeps the original surface exactly where it was.

Tip: Follow it with Decimate if the result is heavier than needed.
menu.status: Remesh (clean solid) — Rebuilds a messy part as ONE clean closed solid of even triangles: overlapping pieces merge, inner walls and small holes in a scan disappear. Use it when a part will not print, bevel, shrinkwrap or cut.

menu.tip:
Wireframe (struts)

Turns a part's edges into round printable struts with balls at the corners — lamp shades, cages, geodesic domes, lightweight lattices, wire sculptures.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. Pick the part whose edges become struts.
  2. Click Wireframe.
  3. Strut thickness (mm) and sides (6 is round enough).
  4. Skip edges flatter than: 1° drops the diagonals of flat faces; 0 keeps every triangle edge.

Tip: Put a Decimate or Remesh inside it to choose the pattern.
menu.status: Wireframe (struts) — Turns a part's edges into round printable struts with balls at the corners — lamp shades, cages, geodesic domes, lightweight lattices, wire sculptures.

menu.tip:
Shell (hollow)

Turns a solid into a hollow shell of even wall thickness — a cup, a case, a lid, a lighter print. One side can be left open.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. Pick the solid to hollow.
  2. Click Shell.
  3. Set the Wall thickness (mm).
  4. Open side: none keeps it closed; top / bottom / ±x / ±y removes the faces looking that way and joins the rims (a cup: open = top).

Tip: A wall thicker than half the part's smallest dimension leaves no room for a cavity; the shell turns red and says so.
menu.status: Shell (hollow) — Turns a solid into a hollow shell of even wall thickness — a cup, a case, a lid, a lighter print. One side can be left open.

menu.tip:
Sculpt (brush strokes)

Pushes the surface about with a brush — Blender's sculpt mode: grab, inflate, smooth, flatten, pinch, and the creature brushes — snake hook (horns, tentacles, spikes), draw, clay strips, layer, elastic grab, pose (bend a limb) and mask.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. (a blend, a subdivided cage or an imported scan works best).
  2. Click Sculpt: the panel opens and the brush is on the 3D view.
  3. Pick the brush, radius and strength, then DRAG over the surface: dabs follow the mouse. Grab, elastic grab and snake hook pull where you drag — a snake hook dragged off the surface pulls a horn out into the air.
  4. Crease and Ridge draw a line along the drag — a wrinkle, a vein, a tendon, a scar. Pose: click the joint, then drag the limb round it. Mask freezes what it covers.
  5. Shift while dragging smooths; [ and ] change the size; a press off the model still orbits. Strokes are kept in Properties: edit or delete any of them later. Skin roughness (Properties) adds pores and lumps over the whole surface.

Tip: Mirror repeats each stroke across the part's middle, so one horn makes two. Add Weathering on top and every crease darkens by itself.
menu.status: Sculpt (brush strokes) — Pushes the surface about with a brush — Blender's sculpt mode: grab, inflate, smooth, flatten, pinch, and the creature brushes — snake hook (horns, tentacles, spikes), draw, clay strips, layer, elastic grab, pose (bend a limb) and mask.

menu.tip:
Displace (scales, cracks, warts)

Gives a surface real skin: every vertex moves along its normal by a pattern — round scales, overlapping shingles, cracks, warts, chitin plates, ridged wrinkles, lumpy noise or a greyscale picture. Like Blender's Displace modifier.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. (a sculpt, a blend, a body).
  2. Click Displace, then pick the pattern in Properties.
  3. Pattern size is how big one scale or wart is; height how far it stands out (negative carves it in — cracks).
  4. Within keeps it to a region (a belly, a back), fading out at the edges; Shingles overlap towards the axis you choose.

Tip: The surface is refined first to an eighth of the pattern size; set Refine to edge coarser if the part gets slow.
menu.status: Displace (scales, cracks, warts) — Gives a surface real skin: every vertex moves along its normal by a pattern — round scales, overlapping shingles, cracks, warts, chitin plates, ridged wrinkles, lumpy noise or a greyscale picture. Like Blender's Displace modifier.

menu.tip:
Shrinkwrap (onto a surface)

Presses one shape onto another: a garment, a cap, a strap or a decal hugs the body under it instead of floating a guessed distance off it — and follows it after a pose or a sculpt.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. Select the piece to wrap FIRST, then the target (Ctrl+click).
  2. Click Shrinkwrap.
  3. Move each vertex: nearest (the closest point of the target) or project (along its normal, or an axis).
  4. Which vertices move: outside (only those inside the target — clothes), all (onto the surface) or inside.
  5. Offset: how far off the surface it sits (mm).

Tip: Blocky piece? Set Refine to split it first, so it can bend.
menu.status: Shrinkwrap (onto a surface) — Presses one shape onto another: a garment, a cap, a strap or a decal hugs the body under it instead of floating a guessed distance off it — and follows it after a pose or a sculpt.

menu.tip:
Symmetry (mirror copy)

Keeps its contents AND their mirror image: model one arm, one ear or one wing and the other half appears — and follows every edit.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view.
  2. Click Symmetry.
  3. Set the mirror plane: its normal (1, 0, 0 = left/right) and a point on it.
menu.status: Symmetry (mirror copy) — Keeps its contents AND their mirror image: model one arm, one ear or one wing and the other half appears — and follows every edit.

menu.tip:
Joint (pivot)

Rotates its contents about a pivot point, like an elbow or a hinge. Joints nest, so a tree of them is a poseable skeleton.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. (e.g. a forearm and hand).
  2. Click Joint.
  3. Put the Pivot on the hinge point, then set the Bend X/Y/Z angles. Min/Max angle limit how far it may bend.
menu.status: Joint (pivot) — Rotates its contents about a pivot point, like an elbow or a hinge. Joints nest, so a tree of them is a poseable skeleton.

menu.tip:
Armature (bones, auto weights)

Gives any body bones so it BENDS — a sculpted or blended monster is one skin, and joints only turn rigid pieces. Like Blender's armature with automatic weights.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. (the whole body).
  2. Click Armature, then add bones in Properties: a name, the bone it hangs from, and its head and tail (mm) — a chain down each limb, the spine, the neck and the tail, heads at the joints.
  3. Pose rows turn a bone about its head (rx, ry, rz) and carry everything below it; the skin follows smoothly.
  4. Falloff makes joints stiffer or softer; smoothing passes make the bend a sleeve instead of a crease.

Tip: Name bones Head, Tail, Left wing, Front left leg… and Send to PlanetCraft walks the creature by its bones.
menu.status: Armature (bones, auto weights) — Gives any body bones so it BENDS — a sculpted or blended monster is one skin, and joints only turn rigid pieces. Like Blender's armature with automatic weights.

menu.tip:
Shape keys (morph targets)

Saved shapes you blend between with a value — a blink, an open mouth, a snarl, a breath. Like Blender's shape keys; a value can be a Customizer slider, so the face moves on screen.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. (a face or a body).
  2. Click Shape keys, then add a key in Properties: a name and a value from 0 to 1 (or a variable).
  3. Key strokes are sculpt strokes with the key's number first: grab an eyelid down, pinch the lips, grab the jaw open.
  4. Turn the value up and the key blends in; several keys add up.

Tip: Use a variable as the value and give it a slider (Variables tab, Customizer [0:0.01:1]): its play button animates the face.
menu.status: Shape keys (morph targets) — Saved shapes you blend between with a value — a blink, an open mouth, a snarl, a breath. Like Blender's shape keys; a value can be a Customizer slider, so the face moves on screen.

menu.tip:
Paint from photo

Colours every face of the selection from a picture projected onto an axis plane — skin, eyes and lips from the photo, a label on a bottle, a livery on a hull. The preview shows it; a print is one colour per part, as before.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. (a sculpted head, a generated mesh, a body).
  2. Click Paint from photo, then in Properties pick the picture and where it sits: plane, lower-left corner and width in mm — the same numbers as a reference image, so line it up with one first.
  3. Faces outside the picture keep their own colour.

Tip: A front photo projects straight through the part, so the back gets it mirrored — add a second Paint with a back photo on the same plane, inside the first, to paint the back properly.
menu.status: Paint from photo — Colours every face of the selection from a picture projected onto an axis plane — skin, eyes and lips from the photo, a label on a bottle, a livery on a hull. The preview shows it; a print is one colour per part, as before.

menu.tip:
Weathering (age, dirt and wear)

Colours the selection by its own shape so it looks old: dirt and shadow settle in every crease, crests rub pale, the surface is blotched and spotted — aged skin, worn leather, a weathered statue, a rusty casting. Like Blender's Dirty Vertex Colors, plus blotches, spots and tints.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. (best on a detailed surface: a sculpted head, a blend at high detail).
  2. Click Weathering; the part keeps its own colour as the base.
  3. In Properties: crease and crest colours and strengths, the depth that gives the full colour, blotches and spots, and tints — a point, a radius and a colour (a red eye rim, a darker nose).

Tip: Sculpt creases and ridges first (Sculpt ▸ Crease / Ridge): weathering darkens every wrinkle by itself.
menu.status: Weathering (age, dirt and wear) — Colours the selection by its own shape so it looks old: dirt and shadow settle in every crease, crests rub pale, the surface is blotched and spotted — aged skin, worn leather, a weathered statue, a rusty casting. Like Blender's Dirty Vertex Colors, plus blotches, spots and tints.

menu.tip:
Hair cap

Grows a thick, curly cap over part of the selection — hair on a head, fur on a back: a skin lifted off the surface by a thickness plus seeded bumps the size of a curl, closed back onto it.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. (the head, a human figure).
  2. Click Hair cap. Set Thickness, Curl height and Curl size; a different Seed gives different curls.
  3. Keep the face clear: the cap skips faces looking within the angle of the chosen direction (-y is the front); two corners in 'Only faces inside' limit it to the skull.

Tip: Colour the cap grey, white or brown with a Color above it; a second cap with a smaller curl over the first reads as a set.
menu.status: Hair cap — Grows a thick, curly cap over part of the selection — hair on a head, fur on a back: a skin lifted off the surface by a thickness plus seeded bumps the size of a curl, closed back onto it.

menu.tip:
Hair strands (fur, manes, beards)

Grows real strands from the surface — a mane, a beard, fur tufts, whiskers — combed, drooping, curled and gathered into locks. Like Blender's hair particles.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. (the head or body).
  2. Click Hair strands: strands grow everywhere except the faces looking forward (-y, the face).
  3. In Properties: how many, how long, root and tip thickness, gravity, curl, locks and how strongly they gather, a comb direction, a region (Only inside), the colour and material.

Tip: A mane reads best as locks: 40-80 locks, gathered 0.6-0.8, a little curl. Use the Fur material for short fur.
menu.status: Hair strands (fur, manes, beards) — Grows real strands from the surface — a mane, a beard, fur tufts, whiskers — combed, drooping, curled and gathered into locks. Like Blender's hair particles.

menu.tip:
Vertex paint (hand painting)

Brush colour onto the model by hand — stripes, war paint, blood, scars, a pale belly, the dark tip of a tail. Like Blender's Vertex Paint.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view..
  2. Click Vertex paint: the paint panel opens and the brush is on the 3D view.
  3. Pick the colour, radius, strength and hardness, then drag over the part. Tick Lines to paint a stripe along the drag.
  4. Strokes are kept in Properties; Undo last stroke takes the last drag back.

Tip: Paint first, then Weathering on top: the creases darken over your paint too.
menu.status: Vertex paint (hand painting) — Brush colour onto the model by hand — stripes, war paint, blood, scars, a pale belly, the dark tip of a tail. Like Blender's Vertex Paint.

menu.tip:
Cloth (drape)

Drops a sheet of cloth over things and lets it settle: a tablecloth over a table, a cape over shoulders, a throw over a sofa, a flag hanging from pinned corners.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. Select the cloth's 2D shape FIRST (a square, a circle, an outline), then what it falls on (Ctrl+click).
  2. Click Cloth.
  3. Friction: how much it clings; Substeps: how little it stretches; Pinned boxes hold the cloth where it starts (a flag's pole side).

Tip: More frames if it has not finished falling.
menu.status: Cloth (drape) — Drops a sheet of cloth over things and lets it settle: a tablecloth over a table, a cape over shoulders, a throw over a sofa, a flag hanging from pinned corners.

items.tip:
Edit vertices (Edit Mode)  Tab

Blender's Edit Mode: the selected part's vertices and edges appear over the 3D view and you shape it by hand — drag vertices, add new ones on an edge or a face, extrude faces out, subdivide, merge, smooth — for the difficult shapes no primitive gives. A part that is not a polyhedron is converted into one first (a cube opens as 8 vertices and 6 faces).

How to use

  1. Select one part, then press Tab over the 3D view (or click Edit vertices).
  2. Click a vertex (Shift adds), a face for its corners, Shift+drag for a box; A selects all.
  3. Drag a vertex to move it, or G / S / R to move, scale, rotate the selection — X, Y or Z keeps it to an axis, Ctrl snaps.
  4. Ctrl+click an edge or a face to add a vertex there; E extrudes the selected faces; right click or W for Subdivide, Merge, Dissolve and Smooth.
  5. Box-model a creature: I insets the selected faces (then the mouse sizes the inner ring), Ctrl+R cuts an edge loop through the edge under the mouse, K draws a knife cut (two clicks); right click for Bridge (two face regions joined by a tube) and Spin (the faces extruded round in steps — a curling horn).
  6. Press Tab (or Esc) when done: the mesh stays an editable polyhedron, saved and written as OpenSCAD's polyhedron().

Tip: O turns on proportional editing so a move drags the neighbourhood smoothly (the wheel sizes it); the panel's Mirror edits both sides of a symmetric shape at once.

  1. Click Skin: a two-point stub appears.
